seed: CREATE TABLE employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, department TEXT, salary INTEGER, manager_id INTEGER, hire_date TEXT, email TEXT, phone TEXT, alt_phone TEXT, emergency_phone TEXT);
CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT, signup_date TEXT);
CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, order_date TEXT, amount INTEGER, status TEXT);
CREATE TABLE products(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, category TEXT, price INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE order_items(order_id INTEGER, product_id INTEGER, qty INTEGER, price INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE logins(user_id INTEGER, login_date TEXT);
CREATE TABLE logins_archive(user_id INTEGER, login_date TEXT);
INSERT INTO logins_archive SELECT * FROM logins;
CREATE TABLE sales_targets(rep TEXT, achieved INTEGER, target INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE customer_records(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, name TEXT, email TEXT, created_at TEXT);
CREATE TABLE daily_sales(sale_date TEXT, amount INTEGER);

exercises.p: Show all columns for employees in the Engineering department, highest salary first.
exercises.sol: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = 'Engineering' ORDER BY salary DESC;
exercises.h: FROM employees → WHERE department = ... → ORDER BY salary DESC
exercises.q: Show all Engineering employees ordered by salary from highest to lowest.

exercises.p: Show each department and how many employees it has.
exercises.sol: SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS employee_count FROM employees GROUP BY department;
exercises.h: GROUP BY department, then COUNT(*)
exercises.q: Count employees in each department, and show only departments with more than 2 employees.

exercises.p: Show only the departments that have more than 2 employees, with the count.
exercises.sol: SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS employee_count FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;
exercises.h: Filter groups with HAVING, not WHERE
exercises.q: Count employees in each department, and show only departments with more than 2 employees.

exercises.p: Return one value: the second highest distinct salary.
exercises.sol: SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);
exercises.h: MAX of salaries below the MAX — or DISTINCT + ORDER BY + LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
exercises.q: Find the second highest distinct salary.

exercises.p: Show name and salary of employees earning more than the average salary.
exercises.sol: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);
exercises.h: Compare to a subquery: (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)
exercises.q: Find employees who earn more than the company's average salary.

exercises.p: Show each department with its highest salary.
exercises.sol: SELECT department, MAX(salary) AS top_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department;
exercises.h: GROUP BY department with MAX(salary)
exercises.q: Find the highest salary in each department (and who earns it).

exercises.p: Show employee name, salary, manager name and manager salary where the employee earns more than their manager.
exercises.sol: SELECT e.name, e.salary, m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
exercises.h: Self join: employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
exercises.q: Find employees whose salary is higher than their manager's salary.

exercises.p: Show order id, customer name, amount and status for every order.
exercises.sol: SELECT o.id, c.name, o.amount, o.status FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;
exercises.h: JOIN customers ON customers.id = orders.customer_id
exercises.q: Show each order with the customer's name.

exercises.p: Show the names of customers who have never placed an order.
exercises.sol: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;
exercises.h: LEFT JOIN orders, keep rows where o.id IS NULL
exercises.q: Find customers who have never placed an order.

exercises.p: Show customer name and number of orders for customers with more than one order.
exercises.sol: SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS orders_count FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
exercises.h: JOIN, GROUP BY customer, HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
exercises.q: Find customers who placed more than one order.

exercises.p: Show the name and total spent of the customer who spent the most on Delivered orders.
exercises.sol: SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS total_spent FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'Delivered' GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY total_spent DESC LIMIT 1;
exercises.h: WHERE status = 'Delivered' → GROUP BY → ORDER BY SUM DESC → LIMIT 1
exercises.q: Find the highest-spending customer, counting only delivered orders.

exercises.p: Remove every row from logins_archive but keep the table. (SQLite has no TRUNCATE — in MySQL you would write TRUNCATE TABLE.)
exercises.sol: DELETE FROM logins_archive;
exercises.chk: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM logins_archive) AS rows_left, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sqlite_master WHERE name = 'logins_archive') AS table_exists;
exercises.h: DELETE FROM table_name; (no WHERE)
exercises.q: A table has 100 million rows. You must remove all rows as fast as possible but keep the table. Which command?

exercises.p: Show name, salary, RANK() and DENSE_RANK() by salary (highest = 1).
exercises.sol: SELECT name, salary, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk FROM employees;
exercises.h: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)
exercises.q: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK when salaries have duplicates?

exercises.p: From subscribers, return COUNT(*), COUNT(email) and COUNT(DISTINCT email) in one row.
exercises.sol: SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(email) AS with_email, COUNT(DISTINCT email) AS unique_emails FROM subscribers;
exercises.h: Three aggregates in one SELECT
exercises.q: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(email) vs COUNT(DISTINCT email) when the column has NULLs and duplicates?

exercises.p: Show each employee's name and first available number: phone, else alt_phone, else emergency_phone, else 'Not available'.
exercises.sol: SELECT name, COALESCE(phone, alt_phone, emergency_phone, 'Not available') AS contact FROM employees;
exercises.h: COALESCE(a, b, c, default)
exercises.q: Show the first available phone number: primary, else alternate, else emergency, else 'Not available'.

exercises.p: Show user_id, login_date and that user's previous login date.
exercises.sol: SELECT user_id, login_date, LAG(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS previous_login FROM logins;
exercises.h: LAG(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date)
exercises.q: Find each user's previous login date.

exercises.p: Show name, salary and a band: 'High' for 90000+, 'Medium' for 50000+, else 'Low'.
exercises.sol: SELECT name, salary, CASE WHEN salary >= 90000 THEN 'High' WHEN salary >= 50000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Low' END AS band FROM employees;
exercises.h: CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END
exercises.q: Label employees as High / Medium / Low salary.

exercises.p: Show rep and achieved/target as a percentage rounded to 2 decimals. A target of 0 must give NULL, not an error.
exercises.sol: SELECT rep, ROUND(100.0 * achieved / NULLIF(target, 0), 2) AS pct FROM sales_targets;
exercises.h: NULLIF(target, 0) and multiply by 100.0
exercises.q: Calculate achieved ÷ target as a percentage without a divide-by-zero error.

exercises.p: In customer_records keep only the newest row (by created_at) for each customer_id; delete the rest.
exercises.sol: DELETE FROM customer_records WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) AS rn FROM customer_records) WHERE rn > 1);
exercises.chk: SELECT id, customer_id, email FROM customer_records ORDER BY id;
exercises.h: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC), delete rn > 1
exercises.q: Delete duplicate customer records but keep the latest one.

exercises.p: Show department, name and salary of the employee(s) with the 2nd highest distinct salary in each department.
exercises.sol: SELECT department, name, salary FROM (SELECT e.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM employees e) WHERE r = 2;
exercises.h: DENSE_RANK() ... PARTITION BY department, keep r = 2
exercises.q: Find the Nth highest salary in each department.

exercises.p: Show customer_id, order id and order_date of each customer's most recent order.
exercises.sol: SELECT customer_id, id, order_date FROM (SELECT o.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS rn FROM orders o) WHERE rn = 1;
exercises.h: ROW_NUMBER() per customer, newest first, keep rn = 1
exercises.q: Get the latest order for each customer.

exercises.p: Show sale_date, amount and a running total of amount by date.
exercises.sol: SELECT sale_date, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) AS running_total FROM daily_sales;
exercises.h: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date)
exercises.q: Calculate a running total of sales by date.

exercises.p: Show month (YYYY-MM), revenue from all orders, and the previous month's revenue.
exercises.sol: SELECT month, revenue, LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue FROM (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY month);
exercises.h: strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) in SQLite (MySQL: DATE_FORMAT)
exercises.q: Compare each month's revenue with the previous month (LAG).

exercises.p: Show category, product name and revenue (qty × price from order_items) for the top 2 products by revenue in each category.
exercises.sol: SELECT category, name, revenue FROM (SELECT p.category, p.name, SUM(i.qty * i.price) AS revenue, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category ORDER BY SUM(i.qty * i.price) DESC, p.name) AS rn FROM order_items i JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id GROUP BY p.id) WHERE rn <= 2;
exercises.h: Aggregate per product, then ROW_NUMBER() per category
exercises.q: Top 3 products by revenue in each category.

exercises.p: Show customer_id and how many rows it has, for customer_ids that appear more than once in customer_records.
exercises.sol: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM customer_records GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
exercises.h: GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
exercises.q: How do you find duplicate rows, and how do you delete them keeping one?

exercises.t: Orders per status in one row
exercises.p: Return one row with the number of Delivered, Pending and Cancelled orders as three columns.
exercises.sol: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status='Delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS delivered, SUM(CASE WHEN status='Pending' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pending, SUM(CASE WHEN status='Cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled FROM orders;
exercises.h: SUM(CASE WHEN status = ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
exercises.q: Count orders per status in one row (pivot with CASE).

exercises.p: Show user_id, streak start date and streak length for streaks of 3 or more consecutive days.
exercises.sol: SELECT user_id, MIN(login_date) AS start_day, COUNT(*) AS streak FROM (SELECT user_id, login_date, date(login_date, '-' || ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) || ' days') AS grp FROM logins) GROUP BY user_id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
exercises.h: date(login_date, '-' || row_number || ' days') is the same for consecutive days
exercises.q: Find users who logged in on 3 consecutive days.

exercises.p: Show the start and end of every gap in invoice numbers.
exercises.sol: SELECT invoice_no + 1 AS gap_start, next_no - 1 AS gap_end FROM (SELECT invoice_no, LEAD(invoice_no) OVER (ORDER BY invoice_no) AS next_no FROM invoices) WHERE next_no - invoice_no > 1;
exercises.h: LEAD(invoice_no) and keep differences > 1
exercises.q: Find gaps in a sequence of invoice numbers.

exercises.p: Show names of customers who bought a Keyboard but never bought a Mouse.
exercises.sol: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id WHERE p.name = 'Keyboard' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o2 JOIN order_items i2 ON i2.order_id = o2.id JOIN products p2 ON p2.id = i2.product_id WHERE o2.customer_id = c.id AND p2.name = 'Mouse');
exercises.h: Join to find Keyboard buyers, NOT EXISTS for Mouse
exercises.q: Customers who bought product A but never product B.

exercises.p: Show name, department, salary and the department's average salary (rounded to 0 decimals) on every row.
exercises.sol: SELECT name, department, salary, ROUND(AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department)) AS dept_avg FROM employees;
exercises.h: AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department)
exercises.q: Show employees with their department's average salary next to them.
